I'm of the opinion that the MOST expensive form of law-making and good-governance is undoing laws that should have never been allowed to pass in the first place! Untold lives have been ruined, families and businesses destroyed, and fortunes made on the backs of lives, families, and businesses, because of corrupt laws and the lawmakers who passed them. Anyone can see, if they care to look, that lawmakers don't take their jobs seriously. In fact, what they are doing decides things like

  1. who lives

  2. who dies

  3. who goes to prison

  4. who walks

  5. what is 'criminal' as opposed to 'unethical' (and there is much that is unethical in government, that ought to be criminal!)

They are literally deciding the lives of millions. The gravity of our lawmakers decisions and severity of the outcomes, impact our entire nation and warrant a process where each lawmaker is given the time and space to focus on one bill to the exclusion of all other distractions until the matter is decided. Likewise, this process, this jury as I've called it, demands the same. Until a bill is submitted by congress, they are free to modify it, debate it, and so on, but these rules act as a break or buffer against unproductive, and otherwise exploitable circumstances--appetites we should restrain for the interest of the nation and posterity.

Why rejudge the bill after a year when it has already passed the process, passed congress, passed the senate, and been signed into law? Isn't that pointless,and inefficient?

The ultimate arbiter of the law should be people. Unfortunately none of us have the time we would like, nor as a nation are we educated enough about the past, to always be watchful and diligent. Mistakes are made, even where a bad bill has managed to pass all these obstacles.

Sometimes too, in the heat of crisis, or national frenzy, we are more susceptible to passing bad laws. And sometimes, we believe a law is necessary but do not have the foresight or hindsight to know it's outcome--and it is only after the fact that we see the law should not have been passed. And so, while the constitution puts a limit on what government may do, and freedom is the right to be left alone, it naturally falls to the people to elucidate, in detail, all the ways in which they would like to be left alone. Likewise we see, the ways in which government naturally expands to fill the apparent ambiguity of it's restraints by passing laws that elide into further laws that expand into powers, and privileges, and exceptions--a behavior that is clear to everyone but those who benefit from it, for reasons obvious to anyone.

** Why 'a' group of jurors, and not the original group?**

To involve as many people as possible in the process, and so that, in the space between the bill passing and rejudging, the original names of the jurors may not be discovered and used to leverage them to uphold a bad bill to the benefit of some political machine or politician.

** Why should it be possible to rejudge a law over and over again because of a mere court case **

Because mistakes are innumerable and chances at hindsight are rare enough as it is. We should err on the side of freedom, on striking down laws, instead of making more. Because new laws can always be made, but the opportunities to undo those laws are both few, and expensive, and the american public fatigue easily. Bad laws by their very nature are far more numerous than good laws. The process to undo bad laws should not be more difficult than the process that created them in the first place, nor should the bar be any higher.

Ultimately, laws should live and exist only as long as is necessary to fix a problem, and no longer.
